reason: The sources contain 12 facts cross-verified across multiple independent sites detailing NGC 772's lopsided spiral structure and tidal interaction with NGC 770.
story: Deep in the constellation Aries lies NGC 772, a peculiar spiral galaxy discovered by astronomer William Herschel in 1785. While most spiral galaxies feature symmetrical, sweeping arms, NGC 772 breaks the rules with a wildly uneven appearance. Gravitational interactions with its dwarf companion galaxy, NGC 770, have violently distorted NGC 772's disk. This cosmic tug-of-war pulled out a single, massive spiral arm that is far more elongated and dominant than the rest of the galaxy. Cataloged as Arp 78 in the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies, NGC 772's gravitational distortion did more than warp its shape—it compressed gas and dust within the dominant arm, igniting active star-forming regions and vibrant stellar nurseries around a bright galactic core. Today, NGC 772 serves as a dramatic example of gravity sculpting galaxies in real time.
angle: Gravitational tugging from a dwarf companion galaxy warped NGC 772 into a lopsided shape dominated by a single, massive spiral arm.

claims.claim: NGC 772 is located in the constellation Aries.
NGC 772 was discovered by astronomer William Herschel.
NGC 772 is designated as Arp 78 in the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies.
NGC 772 has an asymmetrical, deformed spiral shape.
NGC 772 features a single dominant, elongated outer spiral arm that is much more developed than its other arms.
The unusual elongation of NGC 772's main spiral arm was caused by gravitational interaction and tidal forces from a companion galaxy.
The companion galaxy gravitationally interacting with NGC 772 is NGC 770.
NGC 770 is a small dwarf companion galaxy to NGC 772.
NGC 772 has a bright central nucleus.
Gravitational interactions triggered active star-forming regions and stellar nurseries inside NGC 772's main spiral arm.
